Breakdown.Freq.X.text: The Fourier variable represents one homogeneous derivative of velocity. The continuous map into L⁶ recovers the physical velocity and fixes its additive-constant ambiguity.

Breakdown.Freq.bilinX.text: The interaction is defined by its pairings with a heat-smoothed test field. The projected physical nonlinearity is identified with this operator by separate Fourier and velocity identities.

Breakdown.Freq.bilinCompact_holds.text: Compactness is proved for coefficients in the dense span of compact solenoidal test fields. The bilinear bound and operator-norm closure extend it to every coefficient in X.

Breakdown.Freq.mild_holds.text: The formal proof obtains the mild equation from density of Fourier test fields and their Laplacians. The paper uses the cited weak-to-mild theorem for the corresponding physical argument.

Breakdown.orbitNorm.text: A slice below the small-data threshold generates a bounded solution through time one. Uniqueness and recurrence would then force the entire profile to vanish, giving the positive lower norm bound.

Breakdown.IsSimilarityProfile.text: The assumption includes decay of ∇²W and ∇q. Appendix A derives those estimates analytically from the paper’s profile assumptions; that derivation is not supplied by this definition.

Breakdown.monodromy.text: The formal proof subdivides a similarity period until each interval linearisation has norm at most one quarter. Identifying its endpoint product with the paper’s full-period Volterra map uses uniqueness of the linearised equation.

Breakdown.Spectral.exists_dichotomy.text: On the exceptional range, the statement gives a lower bound for forward powers and asserts surjectivity. Together these express the inverse-power decay used in the paper.

Breakdown.orbitSeq.text: Each update is divided by the chosen decay factor. To obtain this recurrence from continuous forcing, first subtract the forcing path at the interval endpoints and then normalise.

Breakdown.exists_section.text: The section lifts the exceptional component into the chosen dense data space. Its values may also have a stable component, which must remain in the forward evolution.

Breakdown.periodicInverse.text: The input is a bounded sequence of continuous paths on short intervals. Proposition 5.3 reconstructs the corresponding continuous weighted right inverse from this discrete mechanism.

Breakdown.contraction.text: The conclusion bounds the initial correction and returns a bounded interval sequence. Its proof chooses the correction from the first component of the right inverse, so membership in the exceptional range also requires that inverse’s range property.

Breakdown.TransferHolds.text: The retained conclusion is existence of arbitrarily close data in a prescribed dense space, with rescaled convergence to the orbit. The paper’s fixed finite-dimensional correction for every nearby datum is a further description of the construction.

Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffGradientClose.text: The estimate keeps a fixed physical cutoff near the centre of the unit torus and lets the remaining time shrink. The large-radius formulation is obtained by expressing the same geometry in similarity coordinates.

Breakdown.Periodic.transplantNorm.text: The periodic norm is the full H¹ norm, so the identity includes μ‖f‖²₂ in addition to ‖∇f‖²₂. The mass contribution tends to zero with μ.

Breakdown.Periodic.transplantField.text: The compact field is placed about (1/2,1/2,1/2) in the unit cell. A spatial translation moves that centre to the origin used in the large-torus exposition.

Breakdown.Periodic.heatDivFreeComparison.text: The formal projected-heat comparison is uniform on a time window $[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}]$. Short times are estimated separately when assembling the inverse; the paper’s Oseen argument gives explicit bounds across the full positive-time range.

Breakdown.Periodic.shellInverseTransfer.text: The theorem eliminates the free shift, solves a reduced equation on the restriction space, and reconstructs the periodic path. Its two comparison bounds and maximum product norm must also be verified when applying it to the continuous weighted spaces.

Breakdown.Periodic.TorusBlowup.text: The intermediate conclusion gives a smooth periodic datum and an unbounded periodic mild trajectory. Two-sided rates and convergence to the physical profile are additional quantitative statements.

Breakdown.Periodic.movingFrameReduction.text: A periodic velocity permits pressure with a spatially affine part. The construction removes that part by a time-dependent velocity shift and translation chosen to preserve the initial datum.

Breakdown.Freq.Internal.GradSixDecay.cut.text: The cutoff is smooth, equals one on the radius-R ball and vanishes outside the radius-2R ball when R > 0. Completion of the physical homogeneous Sobolev space requires the surrounding approximation argument.

Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceDense.smooth.text: The smoothing result starts with an L² field already supported on a compact annulus. Truncating a general field to such annuli and passing to a convergent sequence are separate steps.

Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceDense.symFie.text: A real physical field has Fourier symmetry m(−ξ) = conjugate(m(ξ)). Averaging a symbol with its reflected conjugate imposes this symmetry.

Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceDense.norm_p.text: The transverse projection is contractive at each frequency. Smoothness of projected symbols requires support away from zero, and the error estimate for reality averaging requires a target with the corresponding symmetry.

Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.symbo.text: The result constructs a Schwartz potential for each smooth annular symbol and identifies its curl at nonzero frequencies. Convergence of an approximating sequence also uses the preceding L² approximation estimates.

Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.cutof.text: The cutoff curl is smooth, compactly supported and divergence-free. A separate convergence theorem controls both its gradient error and the gradient error of its negative Laplacian.

For each Schwartz potential and positive error tolerance, the theorem chooses one compact solenoidal approximation. Applying those choices along a sequence gives the approximation used in the exposition.

Breakdown.Freq.longitudinal.text: This is the longitudinal projection ξ⊗ξ/|ξ|². Subtracting it from the identity gives the transverse Leray projection; the real Fourier space also imposes conjugation symmetry.

Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceDense.div_pr.text: The transverse projection has zero contraction with ξ, enforcing the solenoidal Fourier condition. Identifying its output with a physical divergence-free field uses the Fourier correspondence.

Breakdown.Freq.Internal.BilinExists.bili.text: The symmetric trilinear pairing is unchanged when its two velocity inputs are interchanged. Existence of the corresponding bounded bilinear operator and its physical heat-Leray formula are separate results.

Breakdown.Freq.BilinSpec.text: The interaction is specified by all its Hilbert-space pairings. This permits the nonlinear term to be defined without taking a pointwise Fourier transform of each physical product.

Breakdown.compactPiece_of.text: The argument extends endpoint compactness from dense simple coefficients by closedness of compact operators in operator norm. The exposition gives a sequential proof of that general closedness fact.

Breakdown.Freq.Internal.GradSixDecay.mem.text: Inverse-radius decay makes the sixth power integrable in three dimensions. Membership in the full homogeneous gradient space also requires gradient integrability and the embedding result.

Breakdown.HeatBilinear.HasCompactKernel.text: Only compactness on a dense set of coefficients is needed for the transfer argument. The Fourier proof uses frequency restriction, equicontinuity and tail control; the physical-space proof uses local compactness of Sobolev restriction.

Breakdown.Periodic.Cutoff.Internal.hasFD.text: The differentiation theorem concerns the spatial parameter of an integral over [0,1]. Joint smoothness in physical time requires including that additional parameter in the argument.

Breakdown.Periodic.homotopyCurl.text: The identity holds for every smooth divergence-free spatial field and every centre. In the profile construction it is applied to each time slice.

Breakdown.Periodic.Cutoff.Internal.contD.text: The homotopy integrand is smooth in the integration parameter and spatial position for a fixed smooth field. The time-dependent application additionally tracks the smooth dependence of that field on time.

Breakdown.Freq.Internal.VelocityExists.i.text: Closure under addition applies once both summands are known to be compact smooth solenoidal fields. The finite-dimensional section construction supplies that property for the selected correction.

Breakdown.SmoothFlow.smooth_physField_cu.text: The input trajectory has every Sobolev order and satisfies its Fourier integral equation. These hypotheses give smooth physical velocity and pressure, including at the initial time; the full continuation alternative needs additional estimates.

Breakdown.Freq.heatDivFree.text: The output represents one homogeneous derivative of the physical velocity. Its multiplier therefore includes 2π|ξ| alongside the heat factor and the Leray projection; the physical Oseen tensor needs a separate identification.

Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.symbo.text: The weighted curl identities hold almost everywhere, so the single frequency ξ = 0 does not affect them. The measure-zero observation is more general than this particular application.

Breakdown.Periodic.ShellTorus.Internal.v.text: Every coordinate plane has zero three-dimensional volume. Consequently the unit-cell boundary is negligible for Fourier norm identities and for identifying the wrapping map with the identity.

Breakdown.Periodic.ShellDefs.Internal.ad.text: The local transport estimate includes the factor |B|¹ᐟ³ when converting L⁶ data to L² on the support ball. The full radial-extension construction and weighted-path bound need further arguments.

Breakdown.Periodic.InverseAlgebra.Intern.text: For an operator of norm below one, the inverse of I − Q satisfies z − Qz = y. This is the cancellation described by the convergent geometric series in the exposition.
If $\lVert Q\rVert \le q < 1$, the inverse of $I - Q$ has norm at most $(1 - q)^{-1}$. The bound is valid on any Banach space used for the periodic inverse construction.

Breakdown.VarConstIntegralInternal.kern_.text: The assumed singular estimate is restricted to heat time at most one. On longer intervals the proof uses a bound of the form $C_K(r^{-3/4} + 1)$, which still gives integrability.

Breakdown.VarConstIntegralInternal.integ.text: The scalar integral equals 4c¹ᐟ⁴. In the general Duhamel theorem, the quantitative vector bound uses t − a ≤ 1, while integrability and continuity hold on arbitrary finite intervals.

Breakdown.varConstIntegral.text: Integrability and continuity hold on every finite interval. The pure-power norm estimate requires t − a ≤ 1; the continuity proof uses a fixed integration domain and dominated convergence.

Breakdown.Freq.IsWeakSolution.text: The weak-solution class assumes smooth decaying slices and L²-continuous time differences, in addition to the solenoidal test equation and continuity in X. The general physical weak-to-mild statement has a wider input class.

Breakdown.Periodic.ShellTorus.Internal.e.text: The scalar estimate controls (1 + y)e⁻ʸˢ for s > 0 and y ≥ 0. The separate bound involving r¹ᐟ²e⁻ʳ needs its own elementary estimate.
The result is the interpolation inequality ‖f‖₃ ≤ ‖f‖₂¹ᐟ²‖f‖₆¹ᐟ². The period-uniform Sobolev inequality used after it is a separate ingredient.

Breakdown.Periodic.ShellTorus.Internal.s.text: The duality argument treats compactly supported L² forcing after scaling to the unit torus, using the periodic Sobolev estimate and μτ ≤ 1. Extension to arbitrary L³ᐟ² forcing and all periods needs the additional physical argument.

Breakdown.Freq.X.text: The paper describes L⁶ solenoidal fields with L² distributional gradient. The formal space is their derivative-weighted Fourier representation; the velocity map, norm identity and density results establish the correspondence.

Breakdown.Freq.isClosed_sig.text: The formal result proves that the real solenoidal Fourier constraints define a closed subspace of L². This supplies the completeness used by the construction.

Breakdown.Freq.velocity.text: The formal definition selects a bounded linear map from derivative-weighted Fourier data to L⁶ velocity. Its existence and agreement with smooth test fields are proved separately.

Breakdown.Freq.velocity_holds.text: The result constructs the continuous L⁶ velocity map with the required values on compact solenoidal test fields, matching the physical-reading step in the account.

Breakdown.Freq.velocityDecay_holds.text: A smooth decaying solenoidal field, embedded in the Fourier space and then recovered as velocity, agrees almost everywhere with the original field.

Breakdown.Freq.embedNormLinear_holds.text: For a smooth decaying solenoidal field, the squared Fourier-space norm equals the integral of the squared gradient matrix. The embedding also preserves addition, subtraction and real scalar multiplication.

Breakdown.Freq.gradSixDecay.text: The paper’s homogeneous Sobolev inequality applies to the complete physical space. This theorem proves it for smooth decaying fields; density and the continuous velocity map extend the inequality.

Breakdown.Freq.testDense_holds.text: The theorem proves density of compact solenoidal fields and also simultaneous approximation of a field and its negative Laplacian in the gradient norm. The latter is an additional conclusion beyond the paper’s basic density statement.

Breakdown.Freq.testSpan_holds.text: Every vector in the span of embedded compact smooth solenoidal fields is represented by one field of that class, matching the identification used in the density argument.

Breakdown.Freq.niceApprox.text: The formal construction starts from a smooth annular Fourier symbol and returns compact solenoidal approximants controlling both the field and its Laplacian. The account explains the physical vector-potential mechanism behind those choices.

Breakdown.Freq.heat_holds.text: The realised heat flow is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup on X, as in the account. The theorem also states its self-adjointness and its Gaussian Fourier multiplier.

Breakdown.Freq.dilation_holds.text: The theorem gives the exact μ¹ᐟ⁴ norm factor, multiplicative dilation law and covariance DμHμt = HtDμ used in the account.

Breakdown.Freq.dilationCont_holds.text: For each field in X, dilation depends continuously on every positive scale μ, agreeing with Lemma 2.2.

Breakdown.Freq.rotation_holds.text: The orthogonal action is isometric and commutes with heat and dilation. Its Fourier representation agrees with the coordinate changes used in the account.

Breakdown.Freq.bilinX.text: The paper writes the projected physical heat interaction. The formal definition selects the bilinear operator through its Hilbert-space pairings; a separate physical identification relates the two formulas.

Breakdown.Freq.bilin_holds.text: This result proves bilinear existence and the $\tau^{-3/4}$ bound for two inputs in $X$. The additional estimate for arbitrary $L^{3/2}$ forcing in Lemma 2.3 is not included in this conclusion.

Breakdown.Freq.bilinShift_holds.text: The theorem states HsK(τ)(u,v) = K(s + τ)(u,v) for s ≥ 0 and τ > 0, the heat-time shift identity used in the account.

Breakdown.Freq.bilinDilate_holds.text: The theorem states μDμK(μτ)(u,v) = K(τ)(Dμu,Dμv), including the leading factor μ from the change of time scale.

Breakdown.Freq.bilinRotate_holds.text: The interaction commutes with simultaneous orthogonal changes of both inputs and the output, as required by the twisted recurrence.

Breakdown.Freq.bilinCont_holds.text: For fixed inputs in X, the bilinear interaction is continuous for positive heat time, matching the continuity assertion in Lemma 2.3.

Breakdown.Freq.bilinCompact_holds.text: The theorem proves compactness when the coefficient belongs to the dense compact test-field span. The paper’s all-coefficient statement follows after the bilinear norm bound and operator-norm closure are applied.

Breakdown.MildFramework.text: These are the heat, dilation, bilinear and dense-set compactness assumptions used by the transfer argument. The Fourier results prove that the physical equation satisfies them; listing the assumptions alone proves no physical transfer theorem.

Breakdown.MildFramework.IsMildOnIcc.text: A mild solution is a continuous path on [a,b] whose bilinear term is Bochner integrable and whose value equals free heat evolution plus that integral, exactly as in the displayed definition.

Breakdown.varConstIntegral.text: The formal theorem gives integrability and continuity on arbitrary finite intervals, with the explicit 4C_K(t − a)¹ᐟ⁴ bound restricted to t − a ≤ 1. The physical argument obtains the same pure-power bound at every finite length.

Breakdown.pieceOperator.text: The formal result identifies the bilinear integral on one short interval and bounds its operator norm by 4C_KT¹ᐟ⁴ for T ≤ 1. The continuous weighted estimate in the account requires the further summation towards terminal time.

Breakdown.monodromy.text: The formal theorem treats the product of short-interval solves, including their inverse bounds and compact difference from free evolution. The account identifies this product with the paper’s full-period Volterra map by uniqueness.

Breakdown.mildUnique.text: The theorem proves uniqueness for continuous mild solutions with the same initial value on both closed and half-open intervals, matching the account after the Fourier correspondence.

Breakdown.restrict.text: The formal theorem restarts the nonlinear mild equation. The displayed physical identity also allows two independent bilinear input paths, which is a more general integral identity.

Breakdown.concat.text: The theorem combines two consecutive nonlinear Duhamel identities into the identity on their union, exactly the concatenation used to join mild solutions.

Breakdown.mildSmallData.text: The theorem supplies an unspecified positive small-data threshold and a solution bounded by twice its initial norm through time one. The explicit threshold written in the account is an additional calculation from the bilinear bound.

Breakdown.Freq.IsWeakSolution.text: The formal weak-solution condition includes smooth decaying slices and square-integrable, L²-continuous time differences. The physical distributional statement in Lemma 2.8 does not impose those additional hypotheses.

Breakdown.Freq.mild_holds.text: The formal theorem gives the desired mild identity for the embedded velocity under the stronger decay and time-difference assumptions. The paper’s weak-to-mild statement applies to the wider continuous-X test-solution class.

Breakdown.Periodic.V.text: The formal space uses the full $H^1$ norm on a unit torus and retains the constant Fourier mode. The account’s $X_L$ is mean-zero with the homogeneous gradient norm; the transplant identity explains the additional scaled mass term.

Breakdown.Periodic.heat.text: This is the coefficientwise Gaussian heat multiplier on the unit-period Fourier space, as used in the formal periodic construction.

Breakdown.Periodic.kernel.text: This is the symmetric periodic Navier–Stokes bilinear interaction on the weighted Fourier space used for the torus argument.

Breakdown.Periodic.kernelSharpBound_hold.text: The theorem bounds the unit-period Fourier interaction for 0 < τ ≤ 1. The period-uniform physical estimate and its arbitrary-forcing version in the account require additional arguments.

Breakdown.physicalField.text: The formal physical velocity uses terminal time one and an arbitrary initial similarity phase. The account also gives the direct change of variables for general terminal time T.

Breakdown.physicalPressure.text: The formal pressure formula uses terminal time one and a chosen initial phase. The account’s formula permits arbitrary terminal time T, related by physical rescaling.

Breakdown.physicalTimeDeriv_holds.text: After normalising T = 1 and using the same phase, the theorem gives the chain-rule time derivative in Proposition 3.1.

Breakdown.physicalMild_unconditional.text: All supporting analytic implications are proved, but the result still assumes a smooth profile with second-derivative and pressure-gradient decay. Appendix A supplies the analytic bridge from the paper’s less explicit profile premise.

Breakdown.embeddedProfileOrbit_holds.text: The theorem turns the embedded profile into a continuous nonzero recurrent mild orbit, retaining the transformed integral equation and twist. The account also expresses this construction in physical variables for arbitrary T.

Breakdown.orbitBound.text: The theorem gives a finite uniform norm bound for every continuous twisted recurrent orbit, yielding the upper profile bound after physical identification.

Breakdown.orbitNorm.text: The theorem gives one strictly positive lower bound for the orbit norm at all phases. This is the lower bound used in Lemma 3.2.

Breakdown.MildRegular.text: The conclusion supplies smooth physical representatives and finite energy and gradient bounds on a specified closed interval. It does not state the account’s uniform non-increasing energy identity across the entire lifespan.

Breakdown.mildRegular_realization.text: The proved regularity result supplies smooth physical velocity and pressure with intervalwise finite bounds. The account also derives a common initial-energy bound and its monotonicity before blow-up.

Breakdown.EnergyBoundedOn.text: The condition allows one unspecified finite energy bound on [0,T]. The energy identity in the account gives the fixed initial-energy bound at every time before blow-up.

Breakdown.TransferHolds.text: The retained statement gives nearby data in each prescribed dense space and power decay of the rescaled error. The account’s corrected-data family also fixes one finite-dimensional correction space for every nearby datum and adds physical rates and energy conclusions.

Breakdown.transferHolds_of_dichotomy.text: The theorem proves dense-data transfer and rescaled convergence from the spectral splitting. The account’s physical conclusion additionally uses regularity and the Fourier correspondence, and describes the entire nearby-data correction family.

Breakdown.Periodic.smoothPeriodicIsMild_.text: The linked theorem converts a smooth periodic-velocity and periodic-pressure solution into a mild one. The regularity argument for the constructed solution proceeds in the converse direction and is a separate assertion.

Breakdown.breakdownOnSpace_of_profile.text: The global bounded-energy exclusion is the same at every positive viscosity. The formal input explicitly includes second-derivative and pressure-gradient decay, whose derivation from the paper’s assumptions is supplied analytically in Appendix A.

Breakdown.physicalDifference_holds.text: The theorem derives cubic spatial decay for physical time differences from the time-derivative and similarity estimates. These estimates are assembled before the physical mild profile is constructed.

Breakdown.physicalL2_holds.text: Given the physical time-difference estimate, the theorem proves square integrability and L² continuity of those differences. It requires no L² integrability of the individual profile slices.

Breakdown.IsSimilarityProfile.text: The formal assumption explicitly includes |∇²W| and |∇q| decay. The account proves analytic implications supplying those bounds; the profile definition itself does not prove them.

Breakdown.compactPiece.text: The formal theorem proves endpoint compactness from a dense-set compactness assumption in the heat-bilinear setting. The account gives its physical-space instance and a continuous operator-norm approximation argument.

Breakdown.compactSimple.text: This is the first compactness step, for a scalar time path multiplying one fixed coefficient. Arbitrary continuous coefficients are treated by the subsequent density and closure argument.

Breakdown.MildFramework.profilePiece.text: The nth profile piece starts at similarity phase nS/k and restores its local physical scale, as in (4.5).

Breakdown.MildFramework.stepOp.text: The linearisation on the nth interval is twice the bilinear Duhamel interaction with that profile piece, as in (4.6).

Breakdown.MildFramework.stepFree.text: The free interval operator sends the initial vector to its heat trajectory, matching Γ in the short-interval equations.

Breakdown.MildFramework.stepEnd.text: Endpoint evaluation is followed by dilation through e⁻ˢᐟᵏ, matching the rescaled endpoint in (4.6).

Breakdown.stepMap.text: The one-step map is endpoint evaluation after the inverse of I − Aₙ applied to free evolution, exactly the composition in (4.8).

Breakdown.StepDataInternal.exists_step_c.text: The theorem can make the subdivision length smaller than any additional positive threshold while achieving the one-quarter smallness estimate. The account only needs the smallness bound at this stage.

Breakdown.MonodromyStatement.text: The statement describes a product of subdivided interval maps, their inverse bounds and conjugacy, and a compact difference from the free product. The account also proves its identification with the full-period Volterra operator.

Breakdown.Spectral.exists_dichotomy.text: The theorem applies to any compact perturbation of a bounded operator on a real Hilbert space between admissible radii. The paper uses its monodromy instance; exceptional inverse decay is expressed by a forward lower bound and surjectivity.

Breakdown.dichotomyHolds.text: The proved splitting has arbitrary admissible lower and upper radii and applies to every such real compact perturbation. The monodromy application is a special case, with inverse control recovered from the exceptional lower bound and surjectivity.

Breakdown.orbitSeq.text: The definition is the normalised recurrence $x_{n+1} = \theta^{-1}(Mx_n + c_n)$. The account also derives its forcing from a continuous Volterra equation, including endpoint source subtraction.

Breakdown.exists_section.text: The formal conclusion gives a bounded section $J$ with $P_u J = P_u$ and values in any prescribed dense data space. The account expresses the resulting transversal as $E = J(V)$, with $P_u\colon E\to V$ an isomorphism.

Breakdown.SectionInternal.exists_preimag.text: Every vector in a finite-dimensional range has a preimage in the chosen dense linear data space, exactly the density-and-closedness argument used in Lemma 5.2.

Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.tail.text: The negative tail uses bounded normalised forcing and inverse powers on the exceptional projection. The account’s unnormalised forcing formula is obtained by absorbing the factor Θᵐ into each forcing term.

Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.norm.text: For normalised forcing bounded by $R$, the tail is at most $Ar_2^{-1}R/(1 - \Theta/r_2)$. This is the geometric tail estimate used in the weighted inverse construction.

Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.rec_.text: The theorem proves the forward variation-of-constants formula for any bounded linear operator and recurrence. Its application to the stable component is the special case used in the account.

Breakdown.DiscreteDichotomyInternal.step.text: Advancing the normalised negative tail by one step cancels its first forcing term and yields the shifted tail, matching the recurrence calculation.

Breakdown.discreteDichotomy.text: The formal theorem selects the exceptional initial component of a bounded normalised recurrence and bounds all iterates. The account reconstructs a continuous weighted right inverse from those estimates.

Breakdown.periodicInverse.text: The theorem proves the normalised interval-sequence inverse of Lemma 5.4, including a bounded linear output and an initial correction in the exceptional range.

Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement.text: The statement has the same interval inverse, conjugacy, spectral-gap and section assumptions as Lemma 5.4, and returns its bounded-sequence right inverse.

Breakdown.stepData.text: The formal theorem chooses the subdivision, exceptional range, dense-data section and normalised interval inverse together. The account separates these choices and additionally constructs the continuous weighted inverse.

Breakdown.ContractionInternal.exists_sma.text: In a complete normed space, the quadratic growth estimate, the sum-of-norms Lipschitz estimate and 8Kb ≤ 1 yield a fixed point of norm at most 2b, exactly the criterion used in the account.

Breakdown.contraction.text: The theorem solves the normalised sequence correction and bounds its initial correction. It omits the correction’s exceptional-range membership, which follows in the application from the chosen inverse; the continuous residual lemma has a different formulation.

Breakdown.piecePerturbation.text: Adding a perturbation satisfying its quadratic integral equation to a local background mild solution gives an exact local mild solution with the specified initial value.

Breakdown.glue.text: Exact local mild pieces with matching rescaled endpoints produce a mild solution on [0,1), together with the scale identity used to estimate profile convergence.

Breakdown.Periodic.homotopyPotential.text: The homotopy integral is the radial-segment potential in (6.12) and permits any centre. The account uses the special case centred at the origin.

Breakdown.Periodic.homotopyCurl.text: The theorem recovers any smooth divergence-free spatial field as the curl of its smooth homotopy potential, at any centre. The profile argument applies it to each time slice.

Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffField.text: With centre zero and cutoff η(x/r), the definition is exactly the product-rule formula χu + ∇χ × A in (6.14).

Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffDivergenceFree.text: The theorem proves smoothness and zero divergence of the expanded cutoff field once the homotopy identity is supplied. Support and quantitative radius estimates in the paper require additional arguments.

Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffGradientClose.text: The theorem controls the gradient error of a fixed physical cutoff as the remaining time tends to zero. The paper uses a freely chosen expanding cutoff radius and gives an explicit inverse-square-root radius bound.

Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffMassBound.text: The theorem bounds the similarity-coordinate cutoff mass by $K/\sqrt{T - t}$. The paper expresses its mass control using a freely chosen large cutoff radius, with a different parameterisation.

Breakdown.Periodic.transplantNorm.text: With the stated support and scale conditions, the formal identity is exactly the displayed full-H¹ transplant norm formula, including the extra μ‖f‖²₂ mass term.

Breakdown.Periodic.rightInversePerturb.text: The theorem has the same Banach-space maps, one-half perturbation condition and factor-two inverse bound as Lemma 8.9.

Breakdown.Periodic.shellInverseTransfer.text: The theorem retains both restricted comparisons, the common free-shift bound, the factor-four smallness condition and the full inverse norm bound displayed in Lemma 8.10.

Breakdown.Periodic.movingFrameReduction.text: A global smooth viscosity-one solution with periodic velocity yields a solution with the same datum and both velocity and pressure periodic. Periodicity of the original pressure is not assumed.

Breakdown.Periodic.breakdownOnTorus_of_t.text: An unbounded periodic mild trajectory gives the global periodic-velocity nonexistence conclusion for every ν > 0. The result adds neither a rate nor a local physical-profile estimate.

Breakdown.Periodic.breakdownOnTorus_of_p.text: The theorem proves the conditional periodic-velocity nonexistence endpoint from the smooth recurrent profile, including its extra derivative decay assumptions. It does not retain the full quantitative construction described in the paper.

Breakdown.Periodic.glueUnbounded.text: The theorem uses the positive background piece bound, bounded normalised correction and geometric decay of Lemma 9.5 to prove unboundedness. The following two-sided late-time estimate is a further deduction.

Breakdown.Periodic.heatDivFreeComparison.text: The formal theorem gives arbitrarily small error for a restricted rescaled source evolution on $[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}]$. The paper gives an explicit all-positive-time Oseen estimate with $L^{-7/2}$ decay, using a different comparison proof.

Breakdown.Periodic.freeHeatComparison.text: The formal theorem compares a fixed compact solenoidal datum with its unit-torus transplant to any prescribed accuracy, including heat time zero. The account’s large-torus formula gives an explicit $L^{-5/2}$ rate.

Breakdown.Periodic.approxResidualSmall.text: The formal residual is bounded by $KT^{1/4}\theta^n$ on geometric time pieces. The account gives a continuous weighted estimate on a large torus; $T = L^{-2}$ relates their small parameters.

Breakdown.Periodic.torusBlowup_of_parts.text: The formal assembly uses the proved analytic ingredients to obtain an inhomogeneous periodic mild trajectory with unbounded norm. The account also gives explicit continuous estimates and local convergence to the physical profile.

Breakdown.breakdown_on_space.text: The theorem states the conditional whole-space bounded-energy nonexistence result from the smooth recurrent profile. The additional rates and simultaneous construction choices in Theorem A are absent from this endpoint.

Breakdown.breakdown_on_torus.text: The theorem states the conditional periodic-velocity nonexistence result from the smooth recurrent profile. The additional quantitative construction in Theorem A is not part of this endpoint.

topics.name: The blow-up statements
topics.description: Smooth solutions, breakdown on space and on the torus, and the theorems that state them (Theorem 1.1, Theorem 7.1).

topics.name: The fractional extension
topics.description: The authors' separate extension with dissipation exponent between 1 and 5/4, outside the classical paper.

topics.name: Heat flow and mild solutions
topics.description: The heat semigroup, the bilinear Duhamel term, mild solutions, restarting and uniqueness (§3).

topics.name: Recurrent profiles
topics.description: Self-similar time-periodic profiles, their slices and orbits, and weak profiles read as physical fields (§2, §4.1, §7.11).

topics.name: Monodromy and the correction
topics.description: The period map, its compact-plus-small splitting, the spectral projection and the fixed point that corrects a profile to an exact solution (§4).

topics.name: Passing to the torus
topics.description: The solenoidal cutoff, periodization and the periodic right inverse that move the construction onto the torus (§5–6).

topics.name: From certificate to profile
topics.description: Certificate data, the free operator, convection, held solutions and the smoothing of the weak profile they produce (§7).

topics.name: The coercive multiplier estimate
topics.description: The multiplier, its five density coefficients and lower bound, and the a priori estimate it gives (Appendix B.1 and B.2).

topics.name: Encoded cell data
topics.description: The finitely represented inputs: coordinates and harmonics, the profile representation, splines and jets, physical cells, rows, weights and potentials.

topics.name: Reduction to the quarter plane
topics.description: Symmetry reduction of the density to the meridian quarter plane (B.3).

topics.name: Cells, traces and tails
topics.description: Integrability, the common vector of unknowns, resolved modes, the tail budget and the exterior estimate (B.4).

topics.name: Angular and ray-exterior tests
topics.description: The angular inequalities, the pointwise test and the integrated test on ray exteriors (B.5 and B.6).

topics.name: The matrix tree lower bound
topics.description: The tree conditions on the cell matrices and the passage from all cells to the global inequality (B.7 and B.8).

topics.name: Changing the profile
topics.description: Bounds for moving estimates from the reference field to the actual profile (B.9).

topics.name: The adjoint pairing and its error
topics.description: The quadratic adjoint pairing, the azimuthal dual norm and the linear adjoint error with potentials and pins (B.10 to B.12).

topics.name: The offset and the certificate
topics.description: Enclosing the constant, linear and quadratic offset, and the fifteen fields of CellSystemCondition that make the data a certificate (B.13 and B.14).
